common_name: Korsor European Elderberry (Danish Large-Berried Black Elder)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Korsor is self-fertile but sets a heavier crop with a second Sambucus nigra cultivar planted nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Korsor is a Danish selection of European black elder bred for heavy clusters of large, dark, juicy berries and is among the most widely grown cultivars for commercial elderberry juice, syrup, and medicine production in Europe. Broad, flat-topped cymes of creamy white, fragrant flowers open in early summer and are prized for elderflower cordial and fritters, followed by heavy, pendant clusters of large blue-black berries ripening in late summer that are rich in anthocyanins. Korsor grows as a vigorous, multi-stemmed shrub to about 6-8 feet and benefits from renewal pruning of older canes each dormant season to maintain vigor and berry size. Provide consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set for the best yields.
sources: Fern Hill Nursery and Botanical Sanctuary

common_name: Pocahontas Elderberry (University of Missouri Vigorous High-Yield American Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Pocahontas blooms later than most cultivars, so pair it with a similarly late-flowering cultivar for the most reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Pocahontas was selected from a wild population near Pocahontas, Arkansas, and released by the University of Missouri Elderberry Improvement Program in 2019 after multi-year replicated trials showed it consistently out-yielding the widely grown 'Bob Gordon' cultivar. It is the most vigorous and fastest-growing of the university's releases, producing large flower and berry heads on tall, sturdy canes, with flat-topped cymes of white flowers opening later in the season than most American elderberry cultivars, followed by heavy clusters of dark purple-black berries used for syrup, juice, wine, and jelly. As with all American elderberry, Pocahontas spreads by root suckers to form colonies — remove suckers regularly to maintain the desired planting footprint, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to encourage strong new fruiting wood.

common_name: Spring Flurry Allegheny Serviceberry (Upright Central-Leader Tree Form)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; stake loosely for the first season to protect the strong central leader.

directions: Introduced by J. Frank Schmidt & Son as Spring Flurry, this Amelanchier laevis selection was chosen for having one of the best upright tree forms in the genus, with a strong central leader and upward-angled scaffold branches supporting a delicate, oval canopy that sets it apart from the multi-stemmed, shrubby habit typical of seedling serviceberries. Clouds of white flowers cover the bare branches in early spring on coppery-bronze new growth that matures to dark green, followed by small, edible blue-black berries in early summer that draw songbirds quickly. Fall color is a strong, consistent orange. Site it in full sun to light shade in moist but well-drained soil for the densest flowering and best form; the reliable central leader makes it especially well suited to street tree plantings and other spots where a uniform, single-trunk small tree is wanted.

common_name: Spring Glory Canadian Serviceberry (Compact Multi-Stemmed Shadblow)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in average to fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; the compact size makes it well suited for planting near utility lines and foundations where a full-sized serviceberry would outgrow the space.

directions: Marketed as Spring Glory, this Amelanchier canadensis selection ('Sprizam') is a Proven Winners introduction valued for its compact, multi-stemmed upright habit — reaching only about 12 feet tall and 6-8 feet wide, notably smaller than the species and most other canadensis cultivars. Fragrant, star-shaped white flowers cover the branches in early spring, with reddish new growth maturing to rich green, followed by edible dark purple berries relished by birds. Fall color turns fiery orange and red. Spring Glory tolerates a range of soil types and urban conditions, including drought and pollution once established, and its restrained size makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, small-space gardens, and sites beneath overhead utility lines where larger serviceberries would need frequent pruning.
